slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction Language modelling Why is it useful? • Grammar or spell checking: Their There are two birds Everything has improve improved • Speech recognition: I will be bassoon dish →I will be back soonish • It’s how large language models (LLMs) work! (see lecture 4) LLMs are trained to predict words LLMs generate text by predicting words 4 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Language modelling Two LM prediction goals • Probability of a sentence or sequence of words W : P(W ) = P(w1, w2, w3, w4, w5..., wn) • Probability of an upcoming word: P(w5|w1, w2, w3, w4) P(wn|w1, w2, ..., wn−1) 6 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams How can we estimate these probabilities? Can we just count and divide? P(meet|Unicorns bring joy and wonder to everyone they) = C(Unicorns bring joy and wonder to everyone they meet) C(Unicorns bring joy and wonder to everyone they) No! Estimated on a corpus Too many possible sentences ⇒We will not see enough data for reliable estimates Let’s rely on the chain rule of probability 7 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Chain rule The chain rule of probabilities expresses the joint probability of a sequence of events as the product of each event’s conditional probability given the preceding events 8 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Chain rule P(B|A) = P(A, B) P(A) conditional probabilities P(A, B) = P(A)P(B|A) rewritten as joint probabilities Generalized to more variables: P(A, B, C, D) = P(A)P(B|A)P(C|A, B)P(D|A, B, C) General chain rule: P(x1, x2, x3, …, xn) = P(x1)P(x2|x1)P(x3|x1, x2)…P(xn|x1, …, xn−1) 9 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Chain rule applied to joint probability of words in sentence P(w1:n) = P(w1)P(w2|w1)P(w3|w1:2)...P(wn|w1:n−1) = n Y k=1 P(wk|w1:k−1) P(Unicorns bring joy and wonder) =P(Unicorns) × P(bring|Unicorns) × P(joy|Unicorns bring) × P(and|Unicorns bring joy) × P(wonder|Unicorns bring joy and) 10 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Markov assumption Before P(Unicorns bring joy and wonder) = P(Unicorns) · P(bring | Unicorns) · P(joy | Unicorns bring) · P(and | Unicorns bring joy) · P(wonder | Unicorns bring joy and) After (3-gram) �P(Unicorns bring joy and wonder) = P(Unicorns) · P(bring | Unicorns) · P(joy | Unicorns bring) · P(and | Unicorns bring joy) · P(wonder |Unicorns bring joy and) ignore use P(Unicorns) · P(bring | Unicorns) · P(joy | Unicorns bring) · P(and | bring joy) · P(wonder | joy and) Adapted from with the help of Gemini. 11 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Markov assumption P(wonder|Unicorns bring joy and ) ≈P(wonder|and) bigram P(wn) ≈P(wn|wn−1) P(w1:n) ≈ n Y k=1 P(wk|wk−1) P(wn|w1:n) ≈P(wn|wn−N+1:n−1) N-gram where N = 2 for bigrams, N = 3 for trigrams, etc. 12 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Unigram model P(w1, ..., wn) = Y i P(wi) P(wi|w1:n) = P(wi) Automatically generated sentences from unigram models To him swallowed confess hear both . Which . Of save on trail for are ay device and rote life have Hill he late speaks ; or ! a more to leg less ﬁrst you enter 13 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Bigram model P(w1, ..., wn) = n Y k=1 P(wk|wk−1) P(wi|w1:n) = P(wi|wi−1) Automatically generated sentences from bigram models Why dost stand forth thy canopy, forsooth; he is this palpable hit the King Henry. Live king. Follow. What means, sir. I confess she? then all sorts, he is trim, captain. 14 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) • estimates parameters of a model M from a training set T • maximizes the likelihood of T given M Intuition • Suppose the word bagel occurs 400 times in a corpus of a million words • What is the probability that a random word from some other text will be bagel? • MLE estimate: 400 1,000,000 = 0.0004 • This may be a bad estimate for some other corpus, but it is the estimate that makes it most likely that bagel occurs 400 times in a million word corpus. 15 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams MLE of bigrams P(wn|w1:n) = P(wn|wn−1) P(wn|wn−1) = C(wn−1, wn) P w C(wn−1, w) = C(wn−1, wn) C(wn−1) 16 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Dealing with scale • Multiplying many small numbers may result in underﬂow ⇒Use of log probabilities: log(p1 × p2 × p3 × p4) = log p1 + log p2 + log p3 + log p4 • If we need probabilities, use exp: p1 × p2 × p3 × p4 = exp(log p1 + log p2 + log p3 + log p4) 17 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: N-grams
slides.content: N-grams Limitations of N-gram models • Long-distance dependencies: The soups that I made from that new cookbook I bought yesterday were amazingly delicious. • Meaning: the probabilities of the words cat and dog are estimated independently. Solution: (large) language models • Can handle long context • Similar words are represented similarly ⇒some meaning is captured See lecture 4 18 NLP: Language modelling

Turning to another page this second letter is searched for and the succeeding letter recorded, etc." 20 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Extrinsic/dowstream evaluation Comparing LM A to LM B: 1. Use them in a task, e.g. machine translation or speech recognition 2. Evaluate performance on the task 3. Compare task accuries for LM A vs LM B Limitations • Expensive and time-consuming • May not generalize to other applications 28 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Intrinsic evaluation: perplexity • Directly measures language model performance at predicting words. • Doesn’t necessarily correspond with real application performance • Gives us a single general metric for language models (including LLMs) 29 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Train vs test set • Model parameters are trained/estimated on a training set. • Model performance is measured on an unseen test set using an evaluation metric (here perplexity). We want to measure generalization to unseen data Choosing the test set Use cases: • Speciﬁc task: the test set should reﬂect the task language (e.g. legal or medical domain) • General purpose: need for diversity in domains, authors etc. Make sure there are no test sentences in the training set. 30 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Dev set • If we repeatedly test on the test set, we might tune the model to its characteristics ⇒Keep it for ﬁnal evaluation • Use a development set for intermediate evaluations 31 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Perplexity Intuition: A good LM prefers "real" sentences. • Assigns higher probability to "real" or "frequently observed" sentences • Assigns lower probability to "word salad" or "rarely observed" sentences 32 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Perplexity Intuition: A good LM can predict upcoming words. • Once upon a ___ • I ordered a pizza with cheese and ___ • I saw a ___                        time 0.9 dream 0.03 midnight 0.02 … giraﬀe 0.0001 … and 1e- 100 33 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation The best LM assigns high probability to the entire test set. Comparing LM A to LM B: • Compute and compare PA(test set) and PB(test set) • The better LM has the higher probability →It is less surprised by the test set 34 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Why not use probability? The probability of a test set depends on its size (longer = less probable) ⇒Need for a per-word metric, normalized by length 35 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Perplexity Perplexity is the inverse probability of the test set, normalized by the number of words: PP(W ) = P(w1w2...wN)−1 N = N s 1 P(w1w2...wN) • Probability range is [0, 1], perplexity range is [1, ∞] • Minimizing perplexity is the same as maximizing probability 36 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Perplexity of bi-gram LMs PP(W ) = N s 1 P(w1w2...wN) = N v u u t N Y i=1 1 P(wi|w1...wi−1) Chain rule = N v u u t N Y i=1 1 P(wi|wi−1) Bigrams 37 NLP: Language modelling

slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Example perplexity scores for the WSJ corpus with 38M words in training and 1.5M words in test. N-gram order unigram bigram trigram Perplexity 962 170 109 38 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Sparsity Shakespeare as corpus • N = 884K tokens, V = 29K types • V 2 = 844M possible bigrams • Bigrams actually occurring: 300K ⇒99.96% of the possible bigrams were never seen (have zero entries in the table) • That sparsity is even worse for 4-grams 40 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Generalization Training sentences • … ate lunch • … ate dinner • … ate a • … ate the Test sentences • … ate lunch • … ate breakfast p(breakfast|ate) = 0 41 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Zero probabilities • 0 probability bigrams lead to assigning 0 probability to the test set • Which means that we cannot compute perplexity (division by zero)! PP(W ) = N v u u t N Y i=1 1 P(wi|wi−1) 42 NLP: Language modelling

slides.content: Smoothing Smoothing Sparse statistics C(w|denied the): 3 allegations 2 reports 1 claims 1 request 7 total Smoothing illustration adapted from Dan Klein Steal from the rich to give to the poor 43 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Smoothing Adjusted C(w|denied the) 2.5 allegations 1.5 reports 0.5 claims 0.5 request 2 other 7 total Smoothing illustration adapted from Dan Klein Steal from the rich to give to the poor 43 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Smoothing Add-one/Laplace smoothing MLE : PMLE(wn|wn−1) = C(wn−1, wn) P w C(wn−1, w) Laplace : PLaplace(wn|wn−1) = C(wn−1, wn)+1 P w(C(wn−1, w)+1) = C(wn−1, wn)+1 C(wn−1) + V 44 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Smoothing Add-one smoothing • Is a blunt instrument: it makes very big changes to the counts ⇒Is typically not used for N-gram LMs • Used in NLP applications where the number of zeros is not huge • Alternative: add-k where 0 < k < 1, still does not work well 45 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Backoﬀand Interpolation Backoﬀ If you have good evidence: use trigrams Otherwise bigram Otherwise unigram Interpolation Mix unigram, bigram, trigram Empirically, interpolation works better. 46 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Backoﬀ (Stupid) backoﬀ • Suppose you want: P(pancakes|delicous souﬄé) • If the trigram probability is 0, use the bigram P(pancakes|souﬄé) • If the bigram probability is 0, use the unigram P(pancakes) Sum of all probabilities of the trigram > 1 ⇒need to discount the higher-order ngram probabilities (e.g., Katz backoﬀ) 47 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Interpolation Simple interpolation ˆP(wn|wn−2wn−1) = λ1P(wn|wn−2wn−1) trigram + λ2P(wn|wn−1) bigram + λ3P(wn) unigram where X i λi = 1 48 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Interpolation Lambdas conditioned on context ˆP(wn|wn−2wn−1) = λ1(wn−1 n−2 )P(wn|wn−2wn−1) + λ2(wn−1 n−2 )P(wn|wn−1) + λ3(wn−1 n−2 )P(wn) 48 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Interpolation Interpolation: choosing λs • Fix the N-gram probabilities (on the training data) • Then search for λ s that give largest probability to held-out set 49 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.content: Smoothing Out of vocabulary words • Smoothing does not solve the problem of words unseen in the training data • Out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words (e.g. whale in the exercise) • In practice, low frequency words are replaced by an <UNK> token • Low-frequency words and unseen words are estimated based on <UNK> 50 NLP: Language modelling

slides.content: Summary Summary and outlook N-gram language models • Estimation with MLE • Generation (sampling) • Evaluation with perplexity • Choice of training/test data for generalization • Limitations of MLE and workarounds 52 NLP: Language modelling

slides.title: Summary
slides.content: Summary Summary and outlook Outlook: LLMs • Estimation and generation with neural networks • LLMs capture meaning and can handle long-distance dependencies • Evaluated with (modiﬁed) perplexity • Generalization concerns remain See lecture 4! 53 NLP: Language modelling
